name: Orthodontic functional appliances (Herbst, Twin Block)

lead: Functional appliances such as the Herbst and Twin Block hold the lower jaw forward in children and teens with a Class II bite, where the lower jaw sits behind the upper. The payoff is a better-balanced profile and bite while the face is still growing.

The Herbst uses telescoping rods fixed to the teeth; the Twin Block uses removable interlocking bite plates. The Twin Block was studied in a multicentre randomized trial in the United Kingdom in children aged 8 to 10. Research, including a systematic review, separates small amounts of extra lower-jaw growth and upper-jaw restraint from movement of the teeth themselves.

paras: An orthodontist fits the appliance, usually before or around the pubertal growth spurt. The Herbst is fixed, so it does not depend on remembering to wear it, and treatment typically runs for several months. The Twin Block is removable and worn as directed. Forum users ask about cost, adult use and cheaper substitutes.

Reported effects include initial discomfort, chewing and speech difficulty, spacing between teeth, and possible gum or root effects with heavy tooth movement. The appliances are designed for growing patients, and skeletal change in adults is limited without surgery. Over-the-counter substitutes have not been studied for this purpose.

web.title: Orthodontic functional appliances (Herbst, Twin Block) — Grokipedia

chain: Lower jaw grows or shifts forward
angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens, so the jaw grows or shifts forward and the profile and bite balance out. Randomized trials in adolescents have studied them, with debate over how much change is jaw growth versus tooth movement. Adult use for facial appearance is based on user reports.

lead: Orthodontic functional appliances are devices that hold or guide the lower jaw forward in growing children and adolescents, mainly to treat Class II malocclusion, in which the lower jaw sits behind the upper one and the upper front teeth overlap the lower ones.[1][2] For appearance, the aim is to correct the overbite and improve the Class II facial profile, bringing the lower face and chin into better balance with the upper face; Wikipedia describes the Herbst appliance as correcting a dental Class II to Class I while improving the classic Class II profile.[1]

The two best-known examples are the Herbst appliance, a fixed device with telescoping rods attached to the molars and premolars, and the Twin Block, a removable pair of acrylic bite plates.[1][3] Other types include the Frankel FR-2, the Bionator, the Activator and spring-based bite jumpers such as the Forsus.[4][2][1] They are prescribed and fitted by orthodontists, usually around the pubertal growth spurt, and are often followed by braces.[2][1]

The Herbst appliance was developed by the German orthodontist Emil Herbst in the early 1900s and reintroduced in modern form by Hans Pancherz in 1979.[1][5] Research includes cephalometric studies from the late 1970s, randomised trials of the Twin Block and of Herbst versus Twin Block in the early 2000s, and systematic reviews and meta-analyses examining how much of the correction comes from extra lower-jaw growth and how much from tooth movement.[6][3][7][8][9][10]

In looksmaxxing communities the devices are discussed as a way to advance a recessed lower jaw during the teenage years, with questions about cost, access, whether they affect the upper jaw, and whether adults or home-made alternatives can achieve similar changes.[11][12][13]

paras: Class II malocclusion is defined by the upper first molar sitting forward of its normal position relative to the lower molar, and is associated with retrognathia or micrognathia of the lower jaw, overjet and overbite; Wikipedia lists functional appliances, headgear, orthodontic camouflage and fixed braces among treatment options, with surgery once growth is complete.[2][14]

Functional appliances work by changing the position of the lower jaw during chewing and rest so that muscles, jaw joint and growth sites respond. Wikipedia names the Activator, Bionator, Herbst, Frankel and Twin Block among them and calls the Twin Block the most widely used.[2]

The Herbst appliance is anchored to teeth by bands, acrylic bites or stainless steel crowns, typically on the upper molars and lower premolars, and a telescoping rod on each side lets the mouth open while holding the lower jaw forward when closed.[1] Because it is fixed and works around the clock, it does not rely on the patient remembering to wear it, and Wikipedia gives treatment times of about 6 to 8 months against 2 to 4 years for removable alternatives.[1] Orthodontists can add bushings to lengthen the rod for gradual advancement.[1]

Variants include cast and acrylic splint versions, a ball-joint version, combination with a palatal expander, the spring-based Sabbagh Spring, Powerscope and Cantilever Bite Jumper, and versions anchored to mini-screws.[1][15][16] The Forsus and similar fatigue-resistant springs are compared with Herbst in meta-analyses.[9]

The Twin Block consists of upper and lower removable acrylic plates with interlocking inclined bite blocks that guide the lower jaw forward when the patient closes.[3] The Frankel FR-2 and Bionator are other removable designs that have been compared with it.[4]

Emil Herbst, a German orthodontist, developed the appliance in the early 1900s.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, gives 1905 and 1909 for its presentation in Berlin, reports that he described it in a 1910 atlas, and says adoption stayed limited because fabrication was complex and removable appliances were preferred; this should be read with that caveat.[17] A 1994 review in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics summarised current Herbst appliance therapy.[18]

In 1979 Hans Pancherz published a cephalometric study of 20 growing boys with Class II Division 1 malocclusion, ten treated with the Herbst appliance for six months and ten as controls, which began its modern revival using the first molars and first bicuspids as anchor teeth.[5][1] A 1982 study of 42 Class II cases, 22 treated for six months with the Herbst and 20 controls, quantified the skeletal and dental changes behind the correction.[6] Later work examined the jaw joint, glenoid fossa remodelling and biological effects.[19][20][21]

The Twin Block was compared with the Frankel appliance and untreated controls in 1999 and tested in a multicentre randomised trial reported in 2003, alongside a randomised comparison of Herbst and Twin Block.[4][3][7]

Proponents of functional appliances propose that holding the lower jaw forward during growth stimulates remodelling at the jaw joint and additional mandibular growth. The early Herbst cephalometric studies in boys reported changes in occlusion and jaw relationships over six months, with contributions from both skeletal and dental changes.[5][6] MRI and radiographic work followed the temporomandibular joint during treatment in adolescents and young adults.[21]

Orthodontic literature distinguishes skeletal effects (changes in jaw size or position) from dentoalveolar effects such as upper molars moving backward and lower front teeth tipping forward.[1][8] Wikipedia says the rod pushes the upper teeth backward and the lower teeth forward and restrains the upper arch.[1] A trial of stepwise versus maximum advancement examined condylar growth and mandibular positioning.[22]

Orthodontists discuss timing relative to the pubertal growth spurt. Wikipedia reports that treatment before the peak can give normal skeletal and soft-tissue form at a young age but requires longer retention, while starting at or just after the peak is associated with greater condylar growth, a shorter retention phase and less relapse; some researchers found similar results before and after puberty.[1] A cephalometric study of Twin Block timing compared two groups at different skeletal maturation stages, and trials have compared prepubertal and postpubertal Herbst treatment.[23][24] Wikipedia's malocclusion article says functional appliances are ideally used during pre-adolescent pubertal growth and followed by fixed braces.[2]

The UK multicentre randomised trial allocated 174 children aged 8 to 10 with Class II Division 1 malocclusion to a Twin Block or to no treatment and assessed them after 15 months. A summary of the paper reports that treatment reduced overjet and improved molar relationships and that most of the change was dental or alveolar, with a smaller skeletal contribution.[3] A separate randomised trial compared the Herbst with the Twin Block.[7]

A 2006 systematic review of 22 studies (four randomised and 18 controlled trials) reported that two-thirds of the samples showed a clinically significant extra increase of more than 2.0 mm in total mandibular length compared with untreated controls.[8] A 2022 meta-analysis of nine studies (298 patients) comparing Herbst, Forsus and Class II elastics found Herbst gave 1.5 mm more mandibular length than elastics, with no differences in most other measures.[9] A 2024 meta-analysis of 12 studies (574 patients) found a greater increase in mandibular body length with the Herbst than the Twin Block (weighted mean difference 1.44 mm).[10] A 2026 systematic review of 90 studies collated mandibular length changes, with the Twin Block the most frequently assessed appliance (783 patients) followed by the Frankel (573).[25]

Registered trials compare Herbst with different anchorage types, with and without mini-implants, and against the Twin Block; study effects before and after puberty; and examine airway dimensions.[26][15][24][27][28][29][30][16] A randomised trial compared airway and tongue space after Herbst and AdvanSync treatment.[31] Evidence in adults is limited; Herbst-type devices have been tested as mandibular advancement devices in obstructive sleep apnea.[32][33]

Wikipedia reports that unwanted spacing in the upper arch may occur and that patients can have initial discomfort or chewing difficulty during the first weeks.[1] Grokipedia lists speech difficulty, soft-tissue irritation, plaque build-up, root resorption, gum recession with excessive tooth movement, and rod or pin breakage, and describes cost as higher than the Twin Block; these figures come from an AI-generated source.[17] Meta-analyses note that part of the correction is dental, such as lower incisor proclination.[9][10]

On looksmax.org, teenagers with a recessed jaw or overbite ask how to obtain a Herbst appliance and whether it will affect the upper jaw.[11][12] One 15-year-old poster described a short mandible and overbite, said a Herbst seemed out of budget (about 500 euro) where he lived, and asked about alternatives and whether a similar device could be built at home; a reply pointed toward over-the-counter mouth guards.[11] Other threads ask whether Herbst, Twin Block or Bionator appliances change the lower third of the face, or whether a Forsus can be used without an obvious overbite.[13][34]

One thread asserts that Herbst appliances and elastics restrain upper-jaw growth, while in another thread a user asking whether a Herbst would recess the maxilla was told it would not; replies in forum threads advise consulting an orthodontist.[35][12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, functional appliances are discussed mainly by teenagers and parents weighing jaw-growth modification against later surgery, alongside questions about cost, access and substitutes.[11][12][13]

claims.claim: A Herbst appliance can lengthen a short lower jaw and fix a recessed look
Herbst appliances and elastics stunt upper-jaw growth
Cheap mouth guards or home-made devices can substitute for a Herbst
Functional appliances can improve the lower third in people who are no longer growing

timeline.event: Emil Herbst develops the appliance and presents it in Berlin (dates vary between sources).[17][1]
Hans Pancherz publishes a cephalometric study of Herbst treatment in 20 boys, reintroducing the banded appliance.[5][1]
A cephalometric study of 42 Class II cases quantifies the skeletal and dental changes of Herbst treatment.[6]
A review describes the Herbst appliance's biologic effects and clinical use.[19]
A Herbst mandibular advancement device is studied in obstructive sleep apnea.[32]
The Twin Block and Frankel FR-2 are compared with untreated Class II controls; TMJ remodelling is studied during Herbst treatment.[4][21]
A cephalometric study examines Twin Block treatment timing by skeletal maturation.[23]
A UK multicentre randomised trial of the Twin Block and a randomised Herbst versus Twin Block trial are published.[3][7]
A systematic review of 22 studies assesses mandibular changes with functional appliances.[8]
Meta-analyses compare Herbst with Class II elastics and Forsus, and with the Twin Block.[9][10]
